transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Um… yeah. I came because work got really bad, I guess. I’m a waitress, and during service I’ve been sort of… freezing. Like right in the middle of everything, when I’m supposed to be closing checks or running food or answering someone, I’ll just stop.

And it scared people, I think. One time I was standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key, just standing there, and I kept repeating table numbers out loud instead of actually closing the checks. Like, “Table 12, table 7, table 12,” and I knew there were things I was supposed to be doing, but I couldn’t get them in the right order. My manager and coworkers were looking at me like they didn’t know what to do.

It’s embarrassing, because I know how to do my job. I’ve done it for a long time. But lately I’ll start doing things out of order or get stuck, and then everyone notices, and that’s why I’m here.
During one of these episodes, do you lose awareness of what’s happening around you?

I don’t think I black out, exactly. I’m still kind of there, like I can see the soda station and hear people moving around and know I’m at work, but it’s like I can’t… connect the next step to the one before it.

Like the thing that scared everyone was, I was holding the cash drawer key, and I should’ve been closing checks, because I know how to do that, I do it all the time. But instead I just stood there repeating table numbers — “table 12, table 7,” like that — and I couldn’t get myself to actually do the thing. Or I’ll start doing parts of service in the wrong order, like I know the steps but they get shuffled around.

So, no, I don’t think I completely lose awareness. It’s more like I freeze and get stuck, and then I realize people are watching me because I’m not moving on.
Right before you freeze, do you suddenly feel a surge of intense fear or panic?

Um… I don’t know. Not like a panic attack, I don’t think. I mean, I get scared after, because I realize I’m standing there and people are looking at me, and then my face gets hot and I’m like, oh no, I’m messing everything up. But right before it happens, I’m not sure I feel this big wave of fear exactly.

It’s more like things just… jam up. Like my brain hits a wall before I even have time to be afraid. Sometimes I can tell I’m getting overwhelmed because there’s too much happening at once — tickets, customers, someone asking me for change, someone else needing a card run — but I don’t know if I’d call it sudden intense fear. It’s not like I think I’m dying or anything. It’s more confusion, or getting stuck, and then the fear comes when I notice I can’t move on and everybody else notices too.
After one of these episodes, do you remember everything that happened during it?

Mostly, yeah… I remember it, but it’s kind of jumbled, if that makes sense. I don’t come out of it and think, “Where am I?” or anything. I can remember being by the soda station, holding the cash drawer key, and knowing I was supposed to be closing checks. I remember saying the table numbers out loud — like table 12 and table 7 — and I remember people looking over because I wasn’t doing what I was supposed to be doing.

But it doesn’t feel like a clean memory, like “first I did this, then I did that.” It’s more like pieces. I remember the wrongness of it, like I knew the steps but they were all out of order in my head. And after, I can usually remember enough to feel embarrassed, because I can picture myself just standing there in the middle of service, repeating numbers instead of actually moving. So I don’t think I lose the whole thing. I remember it… just not in a normal, organized way.
Before these freezing spells started, had you had any head injury?

Um… no, I don’t think so. Not that I can remember. I mean, I’ve bumped my head before like anybody does, on a cabinet or walking into something when I’m rushing, but nothing where I got knocked out or went to the hospital or anything like that.

Before the freezing started, there wasn’t some big accident or fall that I can point to and say, “Oh, it began after that.” At least… not that I know of. If there was something minor, I don’t remember it being important.
During these spells, do you make repetitive movements you don’t mean to, like lip-smacking, picking at things, or fidgeting with your hands?

I don’t think it’s like lip-smacking or picking at my clothes, not that anyone has told me anyway. It’s more… I get stuck, or I start doing the wrong thing over and over in a weird way.

Like the thing that scared people at work was I’d freeze in the middle of service, when everything was busy, and I’d be standing by the soda station with the cash drawer key in my hand, but instead of closing checks like I was supposed to, I’d just be saying table numbers. Like, “twelve… seven… twelve,” or trying to line them up in my head, but not actually doing the next step.

So it’s not really fidgeting, exactly. It’s more that my actions get out of order, and I’m just standing there doing this useless piece of the task while everyone’s waiting. That’s what made people look at me like something was wrong.
Have you heard voices or seen things that other people couldn’t during these episodes?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t really like saying that, because it sounds worse when I say it out loud, but yes. Sometimes I hear something that other people don’t seem to hear.

It’s usually not like a whole conversation or anything. It’ll be this woman’s voice, pretty clear, saying my name, or saying something like I’m doing the count wrong. Like if I’m closing at work and I’m trying to count everything out, or even sometimes when I’m home in the kitchen, I’ll hear it like it’s close by — clear enough that I’ll actually answer. I’ll say, “What?” or I’ll kind of defend myself, like, “No, I’m not, I already counted that,” and then I realize nobody said anything.

That’s the part that makes me feel really embarrassed, because it’s not like I’m just thinking it. It feels like I heard it with my ears for a second. And then I look around and nobody reacted, or I’m by myself, and I’m like… okay, that wasn’t anybody else. So yes, during those times, I have heard a voice. I don’t really see things, at least not that I can think of, but the voice thing has happened.
Does that woman’s voice ever happen when you are not having one of the freezing spells?

Yeah… it can. I mean, it happens around those stuck moments too, but it’s not only then.

Sometimes I’ll be closing at work, doing the count, and I’m not exactly frozen yet — I’m just trying to get through the numbers — and I’ll hear this woman’s voice say my name, or say I’m doing it wrong. And it’s clear enough that I’ll answer before I even think about it, like, “What?” or “No, I counted that already.” Then I look around and nobody else is reacting.

It’s happened at home too, like when I’m in the kitchen. I’ll hear it close by, like someone is right there, and for a second I really think someone said something to me. Then I realize I’m alone, or nobody else heard it, and I feel stupid or kind of scared. So… yes, it’s not only during the freezing spells.
Have you ever had a seizure?

I don’t know. I’ve never been told I had one, if that’s what you mean. Like, nobody has said, “you had a seizure,” and I haven’t been diagnosed with that or anything.

But I guess part of why I’m here is because I’m not always sure what to call these moments. I don’t fall down or shake all over, at least not that I know of, and I don’t remember waking up on the floor or anything like that. It’s more like people tell me I seemed stuck or not responding right, and I’m trying to piece together what happened.

So… if you mean a clear, obvious seizure, I’d say no, not that I know of. But if there are different kinds that don’t look like that, then I’m not really sure.
Before these symptoms started, did you have a fever?

A fever? Um… I don’t think so. Not that I remember, anyway.

I’m trying to think back to when it first started, and I don’t have a memory of being sick like that right before it — like being in bed with a temperature or someone saying I felt hot. But I also wasn’t exactly tracking things carefully at the time, so I don’t want to say it’s impossible. I just don’t remember having a fever before it started.
Did these symptoms start after something very stressful or traumatic happened in your life?

I’m not sure. I’ve tried to think about that because it would make more sense if I could point to one thing and say, “That’s when everything changed,” but I don’t really have a clear event like that in my mind.

I mean, my life has stress, like anyone’s, and sometimes it feels like a lot, especially with work and just trying to keep everything together. But I don’t know that there was some big traumatic thing right before this started. Nothing that I can confidently connect to it, anyway.

It’s more like I noticed things were getting strange, and then later I was trying to work backward and figure out if there was a reason. But I don’t know. I don’t want to say no if I’m forgetting something, but I also don’t want to invent a reason just because I’m supposed to have one.
Have you had any sudden trouble speaking or understanding words?

Sudden trouble speaking or understanding words… I don’t think so, not in the way you probably mean.

Like, I haven’t had a moment where I suddenly couldn’t get words out at all, or where someone was talking and it just turned into nonsense. I mean, sometimes I stumble over what I’m trying to say or I lose my train of thought, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing. It doesn’t feel like my mouth stops working or like I can’t understand English anymore.

So I’d say no, I haven’t noticed that kind of sudden language problem. If there’s a specific kind you’re asking about, I can try to think more carefully, but nothing clear comes to mind.
Have you believed that this woman’s voice was a real person speaking to you, rather than your mind playing tricks on you?

Yeah… at the time it happens, it feels real. That’s the part that scares me a little, honestly.

Like, if I’m closing at work and I’m counting things up, or if I’m at home in the kitchen doing something normal, I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name, or say something like I’m doing the count wrong. And it’s not like just a thought in my own head, at least not in that moment. It’s clear enough that I’ll actually answer, like “What?” or I’ll look around, and then I realize nobody else reacted or there’s nobody there.

Afterward I can kind of talk myself down and think, okay, maybe my mind is messing with me. But right when it happens, I believe someone spoke. It feels like a real person for those few seconds.
Did all of this start suddenly over a few days, rather than gradually?

No, I don’t think it was sudden like over a few days. It feels more like it kind of crept up on me.

If I’m trying to put a timeframe on it, I’d say this whole change in me has been building for maybe about a year and two months now. It started around the time I was asked to take on the evening shift lead responsibilities at work. I don’t mean that one day I was fine and then that job change happened and everything flipped overnight. It was more like… little by little, I started feeling different, and then over time it became harder to ignore.

At first I probably would’ve said it was just stress from having more responsibility, staying later, having to keep track of things and be the person people looked to. But looking back now, it seems like that was around when things began shifting. So no, not a few days. More gradual, over that year or so.
Has anyone ever told you that during one of these spells you were completely unresponsive when they tried to talk to you?

I don’t know if I was completely unresponsive, like totally not hearing them, but people at work have told me I sort of… froze. That’s the word they use a lot. Like in the middle of service, when everything is moving fast, I’d just stop.

One time I guess I was standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key, and instead of closing checks like I was supposed to be doing, I was just repeating table numbers. Like, “twelve, sixteen, twelve,” something like that. And people were trying to get my attention because checks needed to be closed and the drawer needed to be handled, and I wasn’t really doing the steps in the right order.

That’s what scared everyone, I think. Not so much that I was passed out or anything, but that I’d be there, eyes open, holding something important, and not responding normally or not doing what made sense for the situation. Then afterward I’d feel embarrassed because they’d tell me what I was doing and it sounded so strange.
Right before one of these freezing spells, do you ever get a sudden strange smell that other people don’t notice?

I don’t think it’s a smell, no… at least not that I’ve noticed. It’s more that sometimes, especially when I’m closing at work or even just at home in the kitchen, I’ll hear that woman’s voice. Like she’ll say my name, or she’ll say I’m doing the count wrong, and it’s clear enough that I’ll actually answer her before I realize nobody else heard anything.

So right before I freeze, I’m not aware of, like, a strange odor or anything like that. It’s more the voice that catches me off guard.
Has anyone told you that, during one of these spells, you later could not remember part of what happened?

I’m not really sure. Nobody has said it to me in exactly that way, like, “you lost time” or “you couldn’t remember part of it.” Usually what happens is they’ll tell me I was just standing there or not answering right, and then I feel like I have to piece together what they mean from what they saw.

I do remember bits of it, but it’s kind of… fuzzy around the edges, if that makes sense. Like I might remember being in the middle of something, and then remember feeling embarrassed afterward, but I don’t always have a clean, step-by-step memory of everything people say happened. But I don’t know if that’s the same as actually not remembering part of it, or if it’s just because I was overwhelmed and people were talking fast.

So I guess my honest answer is: I’m not sure. I haven’t had someone clearly tell me, “you didn’t remember this whole section afterward.” It’s more that I sometimes feel confused when they describe it.
Do you ever hear that woman’s voice right as you’re falling asleep or waking up?

Not really specifically when I’m falling asleep or waking up, no. At least, that’s not when I notice it most.

It’s more when I’m doing something ordinary but kind of stressful or repetitive, like closing at the restaurant, counting things, trying to make sure the numbers are right, or when I’m at home in the kitchen. I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name, or say something like I’m doing the count wrong. And it feels clear enough in the moment that I’ll actually answer, like, “What?” or I’ll stop and look around before it hits me that nobody else heard anything.

So it’s not like a dream voice as I’m drifting off. It feels more like it happens when I’m awake and trying to focus on something.
Have you ever been diagnosed with epilepsy?

No, I don’t think so. I’ve never been told, like, “you have epilepsy,” or had that put to me as a diagnosis.

I mean, people have asked me questions about the freezing and whether it could be something neurological, I guess, but as far as an actual epilepsy diagnosis, no. Not that I know of.
After one of these freezing spells, do you feel very sleepy?

I don’t really know. I mean, I don’t think I usually feel very sleepy in a strong way afterward, like I need to lie down immediately or I’m going to pass out. It’s more like I feel… off, or embarrassed, or like I’m trying to catch up with what just happened.

Sometimes I feel kind of drained, but I don’t know if I’d call it sleepy exactly. If it happens at work, I’m usually too anxious about whether anyone noticed or whether I messed something up to pay attention to whether I’m tired. I might feel slower for a little bit, like I’m not fully back into the rhythm, but not necessarily like I’m fighting sleep.

So I guess, no, not that I’ve clearly noticed. Not “very sleepy,” anyway.

Yeah… it can. I mean, it happens around those stuck moments too, but it’s not only then.

Sometimes I’ll be closing at work, doing the count, and I’m not exactly frozen yet — I’m just trying to get through the numbers — and I’ll hear this woman’s voice say my name, or say I’m doing it wrong. And it’s clear enough that I’ll answer before I even think about it, like, “What?” or “No, I counted that already.” Then I look around and nobody else is reacting.

It’s happened at home too, like when I’m in the kitchen. I’ll hear it close by, like someone is right there, and for a second I really think someone said something to me. Then I realize I’m alone, or nobody else heard it, and I feel stupid or kind of scared. So… yes, it’s not only during the freezing spells.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a recent seizure, which would strongly support an organic psychotic disorder related to epilepsy over primary psychosis or dissociative symptoms.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of seizures, but the provided symptom profile does not include seizures or seizure history.

patient.answer:
I don’t know. I’ve never been told I had one, if that’s what you mean. Like, nobody has said, “you had a seizure,” and I haven’t been diagnosed with that or anything.

But I guess part of why I’m here is because I’m not always sure what to call these moments. I don’t fall down or shake all over, at least not that I know of, and I don’t remember waking up on the floor or anything like that. It’s more like people tell me I seemed stuck or not responding right, and I’m trying to piece together what happened.

So… if you mean a clear, obvious seizure, I’d say no, not that I know of. But if there are different kinds that don’t look like that, then I’m not really sure.

But I also wasn’t exactly tracking things carefully at the time, so I don’t want to say it’s impossible. I just don’t remember having a fever before it started.

I’m not sure. I’ve tried to think about that because it would make more sense if I could point to one thing and say, “That’s when everything changed,” but I don’t really have a clear event like that in my mind.

I mean, my life has stress, like anyone’s, and sometimes it feels like a lot, especially with work and just trying to keep everything together. But I don’t know that there was some big traumatic thing right before this started. Nothing that I can confidently connect to it, anyway.

It’s more like I noticed things were getting strange, and then later I was trying to work backward and figure out if there was a reason. But I don’t know. I don’t want to say no if I’m forgetting something, but I also don’t want to invent a reason just because I’m supposed to have one.

I mean, sometimes I stumble over what I’m trying to say or I lose my train of thought, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing. So I’d say no, I haven’t noticed that kind of sudden language problem. If there’s a specific kind you’re asking about, I can try to think more carefully, but nothing clear comes to mind.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the auditory hallucinations are accompanied by delusional conviction, which would strongly favor an acute psychotic disorder over seizure-related or dissociative causes.

patient.answer:
Yeah… at the time it happens, it feels real. That’s the part that scares me a little, honestly.

Like, if I’m closing at work and I’m counting things up, or if I’m at home in the kitchen doing something normal, I’ll hear a woman’s voice say my name, or say something like I’m doing the count wrong. And it’s not like just a thought in my own head, at least not in that moment. It’s clear enough that I’ll actually answer, like “What?” or I’ll look around, and then I realize nobody else reacted or there’s nobody there.

Afterward I can kind of talk myself down and think, okay, maybe my mind is messing with me. But right when it happens, I believe someone spoke. It feels like a real person for those few seconds.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms began abruptly and have lasted less than a month, which would strongly support acute psychotic disorder over seizure/dissociative or other organic causes.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think it was sudden like over a few days. It feels more like it kind of crept up on me.

If I’m trying to put a timeframe on it, I’d say this whole change in me has been building for maybe about a year and two months now. It started around the time I was asked to take on the evening shift lead responsibilities at work. I don’t mean that one day I was fine and then that job change happened and everything flipped overnight. It was more like… little by little, I started feeling different, and then over time it became harder to ignore.

At first I probably would’ve said it was just stress from having more responsibility, staying later, having to keep track of things and be the person people looked to. But looking back now, it seems like that was around when things began shifting. So no, not a few days. More gradual, over that year or so.

inference.note: Ruled out F23 because onset was gradual over ~14 months rather than acute over days; persistent auditory hallucinations with episodic freezing/apraxia-like behavior still fit organic hallucinosis/other specified mental disorder due to brain disease or focal seizure spectrum, with dissociative disorder remaining less likely.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I was completely unresponsive, like totally not hearing them, but people at work have told me I sort of… froze. That’s the word they use a lot. Like in the middle of service, when everything is moving fast, I’d just stop.

One time I guess I was standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key, and instead of closing checks like I was supposed to be doing, I was just repeating table numbers. Like, “twelve, sixteen, twelve,” something like that. And people were trying to get my attention because checks needed to be closed and the drawer needed to be handled, and I wasn’t really doing the steps in the right order.

That’s what scared everyone, I think. Not so much that I was passed out or anything, but that I’d be there, eyes open, holding something important, and not responding normally or not doing what made sense for the situation. Then afterward I’d feel embarrassed because they’d tell me what I was doing and it sounded so strange.

I’m not really sure. Nobody has said it to me in exactly that way, like, “you lost time” or “you couldn’t remember part of it.” Usually what happens is they’ll tell me I was just standing there or not answering right, and then I feel like I have to piece together what they mean from what they saw.

I do remember bits of it, but it’s kind of… fuzzy around the edges, if that makes sense. Like I might remember being in the middle of something, and then remember feeling embarrassed afterward, but I don’t always have a clean, step-by-step memory of everything people say happened. But I don’t know if that’s the same as actually not remembering part of it, or if it’s just because I was overwhelmed and people were talking fast.

So I guess my honest answer is: I’m not sure. I haven’t had someone clearly tell me, “you didn’t remember this whole section afterward.” It’s more that I sometimes feel confused when they describe it.

I don’t really know. I mean, I don’t think I usually feel very sleepy in a strong way afterward, like I need to lie down immediately or I’m going to pass out. It’s more like I feel… off, or embarrassed, or like I’m trying to catch up with what just happened.

I might feel slower for a little bit, like I’m not fully back into the rhythm, but not necessarily like I’m fighting sleep.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports persistent auditory hallucinations occurring both during and outside freezing episodes, with preserved partial awareness, gradual onset over about 14 months, and no clear traumatic trigger. This pattern is more consistent with another specified mental disorder due to brain damage/dysfunction/physical disease than with dissociative disorder. Focal seizures remain a differential because of stereotyped freezing and automatism-like repetition, but the prolonged course and inter-episodic psychotic symptoms favor F06.8 over G40.89 based on the available choices.
